result: New hominin footprints were discovered at Site S, located 150 m south of Site G at Laetoli. Fourteen tracks were found in three test pits (L8, M9, TP2), attributed to two individuals: S1 (13 tracks forming a 32 m trackway trending SSE to NNW) and S2 (1 track).
evaluation: Claims C5-C57 provide detailed documentation of the discovery, including excavation methods (C49-C50), spatial distribution (C47-C48, C51-C54), and trackway characteristics (C55-C56). The evidence is based on systematic field observations, measurements, and 3D imaging documented in figures and tables.

result: The Site S tracks were made on the same palaeosurface as Site G tracks, with both sites located on the same morphological terrace. Stratigraphic analysis indicates the tracks were printed on the Footprint Tuff, though exact sublevel correlation between sites remains uncertain due to lack of observable stratigraphic continuity.
evaluation: Claims C7-C8 and C95-C102 establish the geological relationship between sites through field observations and stratigraphic correlation. While C97 acknowledges no direct stratigraphic continuity, C98 and C102 provide evidence for correlation based on unit characteristics. The authors appropriately note uncertainty in fine-scale correlation while supporting same-surface interpretation.

result: The S1 tracks exhibit morphological features consistent with Site G tracks, particularly G2, including oval heel shape, medial arch elevation, 75° ball region orientation, adducted hallux, posterior drag marks, and lateral weight transfer pattern. The angle of gait (2-11°) resembles G2/3 more than G1.
evaluation: Claims C75-C85 provide detailed morphological descriptions supported by 3D imaging data (Figures 2-11) and comparative analysis with Site G tracks. The observations are based on multiple tracks with consistent features. Claims C81-C82 appropriately identify interpretations as inferences rather than direct observations.

result: Morphometric analysis shows S1 tracks (average length 261 mm) are larger than G1-G3 tracks (180-225 mm), with estimated stature of ~165 cm and body mass of ~44.7 kg for S1, and ~146 cm and ~39.5 kg for S2. All individuals walked at similar low speeds (0.44-0.9 m/s).
evaluation: Claims C86-C94 and C103-C104 are supported by detailed measurements in Tables 2-3 and multiple estimation methods. The data show consistent patterns across different analytical approaches. Speed estimates are based on established biomechanical equations (Alexander 1976, Dingwall et al. 2013).

result: The estimated stature of S1 (~165 cm) exceeds all known Au. afarensis specimens from skeletal remains (Hadar: 109-143 cm; Woranso-Mille: 158 cm) and falls within the range of H. erectus and modern H. sapiens. Body mass estimates (41-48 kg) fall within the male Au. afarensis range, identifying S1 as a large-bodied individual, probably male.
evaluation: Claims C10 and C105-C112 are supported by comparative data in Figure 12 and Table 3, with appropriate citations to published skeletal data. The authors acknowledge methodological limitations (C90-C91) regarding use of modern human proportions. The identification as male (C111) is appropriately qualified as probable based on body size distributions from Grabowski et al. 2015.

result: The Laetoli footprints indicate considerable body size variation and probable sexual dimorphism within a single hominin species at 3.66 Ma. Body mass estimates suggest G1 and G3 fall within female ranges (25.5-38.1 kg), G2 and S2 span upper female/lower male ranges (40.2-61.0 kg), and S1 represents a large male. This variation exceeds that previously documented at Hadar (3.2 Ma).
evaluation: Claims C12-C13 and C118-C122 present interpretations based on body size estimates, but several uncertainties limit support: (1) C120 is explicitly labeled as "tentative" and speculative; (2) sex determination relies on body mass ranges from Grabowski et al. 2015 applied to footprint-based estimates with acknowledged methodological limitations (C90-C91); (3) the presence of only one S2 track (acknowledged in manuscript) limits confidence in that individual's characterization; (4) alternative explanations (e.g., multiple species, age variation) are not fully excluded. While the data show size variation, the specific interpretation regarding sexual dimorphism requires additional evidence.

result: The findings support a nonlinear evolutionary trend in hominin body size, with large-bodied individuals present in Au. afarensis from 3.66-3.2 Ma. This contrasts with hypotheses linking the emergence of Homo or dispersal from Africa to abrupt body size increases, and contradicts temporal trends of size increase within Au. afarensis.
evaluation: Claims C113-C116 and C123-C124 are supported by the comparative data in Figure 12 showing overlap between Au. afarensis and later Homo body sizes, with appropriate citations to Grabowski et al. 2015 and Jungers et al. 2016. The temporal span (C123) is well-established by dating. However, the interpretation relies on the assumption that all tracks represent Au. afarensis (C46), which is noted as controversial in the manuscript itself.

result: The trackway evidence suggests at least five individuals (G1, G2, G3, S1, S2) walked together in the same direction at similar speeds, with pronounced body size variation implying a social structure closer to gorillas than chimpanzees or modern humans.
evaluation: Claim C125 regarding contemporaneous walking is supported by geological evidence (C7-C8, C102) and speed estimates (C86), though exact temporal synchrony cannot be definitively established. Claim C127 regarding gorilla-like social structure is explicitly speculative, extrapolating from body size dimorphism to mating systems and social organization without direct behavioral evidence. This interpretation assumes: (1) the size variation reflects sexual dimorphism rather than other factors, (2) modern primate analogies apply to extinct hominins, and (3) all individuals belong to a single social group rather than separate groups using the same path at different times.

result: A total of 529 non-hominin mammal and bird tracks were documented at Site S, including small bovids (likely Madoqua), medium bovids (Gazella/Eudorcas/Nanger), equids, giraffids, rhinoceroses, lagomorphs, and guinea fowl (Numida). This assemblage suggests a mosaic palaeoenvironment of bushland, woodland, grassland, and riverine forest.
evaluation: Claims C68-C74 are supported by systematic documentation in Table 1 and figures showing track morphology. Taxonomic identifications (C69-C73) are appropriately qualified as probable based on size and morphology, with acknowledgment of identification challenges (C71). The palaeoenvironmental interpretation (C74) reasonably follows from the faunal assemblage, though it represents an inference from ichnological data.

result: Track preservation varies considerably across test pits depending on depth of the Footprint Tuff. In L8 (shallow, <20 cm), tracks are poorly preserved with damage from roots and fractures. In M9 (~72 cm deep), tracks are well-preserved, sealed by overlying tuff and filled with cemented sediment. Excavation methods included careful removal of infill matrix using water and dental tools.
evaluation: Claims C58-C67 provide detailed taphonomic observations supported by field photographs (Figures 7-9) and stratigraphic descriptions. The preservation differences are clearly documented and explained by burial depth. Methodological details (C66-C67) are appropriate for understanding data quality and potential biases in morphological analysis.

result: The identification of large-bodied Au. afarensis individuals suggests the fossil record may underestimate hominin phenotypic diversity. Additional hominin trails may exist in the area between Sites G and S.
evaluation: Claim C117 is a reasonable inference from the discovery of S1, which exceeds known skeletal specimens in stature, highlighting preservation biases in the fossil record. Claim C128 is appropriately presented as speculation based on the 150 m separation between sites and the presence of continuous geological units, representing a testable hypothesis for future work.

result: Laetoli is a palaeontological locality in northern Tanzania within the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, known since the 1930s and famous for 3.66 Ma hominin footprints discovered in 1978 at Site G. The Site G trackways show three individuals (G1, G2, G3) attributed to Au. afarensis, the only hominin taxon found in the Upper Laetoli Beds.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4 and C33-C46 provide established background information supported by extensive citations to prior work (Leakey 1981, 1987; Hay 1987; Deino 2011; Harrison 2011; White and Suwa 1987). The 3.66 Ma age (C2, C39) is well-established by Deino 2011. The attribution to Au. afarensis (C4, C46) is noted as controversial (Tuttle et al. 1991; Harcourt-Smith 2005) but represents the consensus view.

result: Body size estimates are crucial for understanding hominin evolution and have been debated since the 1970s. Within-species variation relates to sexual dimorphism and ecological adaptation. For Au. afarensis, there is ongoing debate about the degree of sexual dimorphism, with some studies supporting pronounced dimorphism and others moderate dimorphism.
evaluation: Claims C14-C32 provide appropriate literature review and context, accurately representing the state of debate in the field with balanced citations to opposing views (e.g., Richmond and Jungers 1995 vs. Reno et al. 2003; Grabowski et al. 2015). These claims establish the scientific rationale for the study.

result: Fieldwork was conducted under permit from the Ngorongoro Conservation Area Authority. Stature estimation methods used foot:stature ratios of 14-16% for H. sapiens and 15.5-16.2% for Au. afarensis. The transitional speed from walk to run is ~2.2 m/s.
evaluation: Claims C129-C132 provide essential methodological information. The permit documentation (C129) establishes legal compliance. The anthropometric ratios (C130-C131) and biomechanical parameters (C132) are appropriately cited to established literature (Tuttle 1987; Dingwall et al. 2013) and are standard values used in the field.
